blocks.html: A food is unsafe when something in it can make a person sick or hurt. Kitchens sort those dangers into three kinds, because each is prevented a different way.

Biological hazards: bacteria, viruses and parasites, and the toxins some bacteria make. Chemical hazards: cleaning chemicals, pesticides, too much of an additive, and food allergens. Physical hazards: objects such as glass, metal shavings, bone, plastic or a bandage. Most foodborne illness comes from biological hazards.

head: Bacteria need
So the kitchen…
rows: treats meat, dairy, eggs, cooked rice, cut melons and cut leafy greens as foods that need time and temperature control
keeps food out of the danger zone, 41°F to 135°F
limits how long food stays warm
knows dry foods (crackers, flour) are lower risk
follows tested recipes for pickles and sealed foods

blocks.html: Foods that support fast growth of germs are called TCS foods in the Food Code: foods that need Time and Temperature Control for Safety. Cooked rice, cut tomatoes and cut leafy greens are on that list, not just meat.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: A chip of glass from a broken jar falls into a salad.
steps: It is an object, not a germ or a chemical.
blocks.a: A physical hazard. Throw the salad away.

blocks.html: Thinking you can smell or see unsafe food. The germs that cause most illness usually don't change the smell, look or taste of food. Spoilage germs do, but they are a different group.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Look through your refrigerator and list the TCS foods: cooked leftovers, dairy, eggs, meat, cut fruit. These are the ones to watch for time and temperature.

blocks.html: Bacteria multiply fastest at warm temperatures. Below about 41°F they slow down a lot; above about 135°F most stop growing. In between is the temperature danger zone.

For restaurants, the FDA Food Code says: hold cold TCS food at 41°F or below and hot TCS food at 135°F or above. For home cooks, USDA describes the danger zone as 40°F to 140°F and says not to leave perishable food out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F).

blocks.name: cu-cool
blocks.cap: The danger zone on a thermometer: the Food Code's 41°F to 135°F, and USDA's 40°F to 140°F for home cooks.

blocks.html: Why two sets of numbers? They come from different documents written for different readers. The Food Code is a model code that state and local health departments adopt for restaurants and stores; USDA's numbers are a simple, cautious message for home kitchens. They agree on the point that matters: keep food out of the middle, and move it through quickly when cooking or cooling.

blocks.title: In or out?
blocks.q: A tray of cooked chicken on a buffet reads 128°F. Is it in the danger zone by the Food Code?
steps: Hot holding must be 135°F or above.
128°F is below that.
blocks.a: Yes: it is in the danger zone and must be reheated or handled by the kitchen's rules.

blocks.html: Thinking the refrigerator makes food safe forever. Cold slows bacteria but does not kill them; that is why ready-to-eat food has a time limit even when cold.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Put a thermometer in a glass of water in your refrigerator overnight. Is it at 40°F or below? Check the freezer is at 0°F.

blocks.html: Cooking kills germs when the food reaches a high enough temperature, held for long enough. The only reliable test is a thermometer in the thickest part of the food.

USDA safe minimum internal temperatures (for consumers): poultry, whole or ground, 165°F; ground beef, pork, veal and lamb 160°F; egg dishes 160°F; beef, pork, veal and lamb steaks, chops and roasts 145°F with a 3-minute rest; fish 145°F; leftovers and casseroles 165°F. The Food Code (for restaurants) pairs temperatures with times: for example 145°F for 15 seconds (whole cuts, fish, eggs cooked to order), 155°F for 17 seconds (ground meat), 165°F for under 1 second (poultry).

head: Food
USDA (home)
Food Code (restaurants)
rows: Chicken, turkey, duck (whole, parts, ground); stuffing
155°F for 17 seconds (or 158°F instantly, 150°F for 1 minute, 145°F for 3 minutes)
Steaks, chops, roasts (beef, pork, veal, lamb)
145°F for 15 seconds; whole roasts by a time table
145°F, or opaque and flakes with a fork
Cook until yolk and white are firm; egg dishes 160°F

blocks.name: cu-temps
blocks.cap: Test yourself: pick the USDA safe minimum temperature for each food.

blocks.html: Why is ground beef higher than a steak? On a whole steak, germs live on the surface, which gets very hot when seared. Grinding mixes the surface into the middle, so the center must get hot too. Poultry is highest because of germs such as Salmonella that can be all through it.

blocks.title: Is it done?
blocks.q: A chicken thigh reads 158°F in the thickest part, away from the bone.
steps: Poultry must reach 165°F.
blocks.a: Not yet: keep cooking and check again.

blocks.html: Checking the thin end or touching bone with the probe. Bone conducts heat differently. Put the tip in the center of the thickest part.

🛡️ Safety

  • Restaurants that serve food rarer than these temperatures (a rare burger, raw oysters, a soft egg) must tell customers in writing, by the Food Code's consumer advisory rule; some foods, such as undercooked ground meat, may not be served that way to highly susceptible groups.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Cook a chicken breast and check it in three places. Write down all three readings and notice how much they differ.

blocks.html: Hot food has to pass through the danger zone to get cold. The bigger the batch, the slower it cools, and a big pot in a refrigerator can stay warm in the middle for many hours.

The Food Code's two-stage cooling rule: cool cooked TCS food from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then from 70°F to 41°F or below within the next 4 hours: 6 hours in all. The first stage is the strict one, because bacteria grow fastest between about 125°F and 70°F.

blocks.name: cu-cool
blocks.cap: Set when the food reached 70°F and 41°F, or try a cooling method, and see if it passes.

head: Method (Food Code 3-501.15)
Why it works
rows: Shallow pans (food about 2 inches deep or less), uncovered or loosely covered until cold
More surface, less distance for heat to travel
Cut large items into smaller pieces
Water pulls heat far faster than air
Ice added as an ingredient (for soups and stocks)
The ice replaces some of the water in the recipe
Fast cold air or water made for cooling

blocks.html: If food reaches 70°F early, say in 1 hour, the FDA's handout says the remaining time still applies to reaching 41°F; the 6 hours in total is the outer limit. If food is not at 70°F within 2 hours, the Food Code says it must be reheated to 165°F and cooled again from the start, or thrown away, depending on the rules where you work.

blocks.title: Did it pass?
blocks.q: Chili is 135°F at noon, 72°F at 2:00 p.m., and 40°F at 5:00 p.m.
steps: Stage 1: 135°F to 70°F must happen by 2:00 p.m. At 2:00 it was 72°F, still above 70°F.
Stage 1 failed, even though stage 2 was fast.

blocks.title: Time left
blocks.q: Stock reaches 70°F 90 minutes after it was 135°F. By when must it reach 41°F, counting from 135°F?
steps: 6 hours in all from 135°F.
It reached 70°F at 1.5 hours; the outer limit is 6 hours from the start.
blocks.a: Within 6 hours of the start (4½ hours after it hit 70°F).

blocks.html: Putting a lid on a deep, hot pot and putting it in the walk-in. The lid traps heat, the pot holds it, and warm air from it can warm nearby food.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Make a pot of stock or soup. Split it: one half stays in the pot in the refrigerator; the other goes into a shallow pan set in an ice bath. Check both temperatures every 30 minutes for 2 hours and graph them.

blocks.html: Food in a kitchen spends a lot of its life waiting: in the steam table, the walk-in, a prep container. The Food Code sets rules for each kind of waiting.

Hot holding: 135°F or above. Cold holding: 41°F or below. Reheating for hot holding: food cooked and cooled in the kitchen is reheated so all parts reach 165°F for 15 seconds, within 2 hours. Date marking: ready-to-eat TCS food kept more than 24 hours is labeled and used or thrown away within 7 days at 41°F, counting the day it was made as day 1. FIFO: first in, first out.

items: Label every container: what it is, the date made, and the use-by date (and your initials, in many kitchens).
Put new deliveries behind or under older stock, so the older is used first.
Check hot and cold holding temperatures on a schedule, and write them down.
Steam tables and hot-holding cabinets are made to keep hot food hot, not to heat cold food; reheat on the range, in an oven or a microwave first.

blocks.html: Seven days is a limit for slow-growing germs such as Listeria, which can grow even in the cold. It is a safety limit, not a quality promise: many foods taste stale long before day 7.

blocks.title: Use-by date
blocks.q: Chicken salad is made on Monday, March 3. What is the last day to use it under the 7-day rule (made day counts as day 1)?
steps: Day 1 is March 3. Day 7 is March 9.

blocks.title: Reheating
blocks.q: Leftover soup from yesterday goes into the steam table at lunch. What must happen first?
steps: Reheat so all of it reaches 165°F for 15 seconds, within 2 hours.
Then hold at 135°F or above.
blocks.a: Reheat to 165°F, then hold at 135°F or above.

blocks.html: Putting cold food straight into the steam table to "warm up". It spends far too long in the danger zone.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Label everything in your refrigerator with masking tape: what it is and the date. After a week, see what you threw away and why.

blocks.html: Germs don't move on their own; we move them: on hands, boards, knives, towels, and drips from one food onto another.

Separate raw from ready-to-eat. Use separate boards and knives (or clean and sanitize between), wash hands after touching raw meat, and store food in the refrigerator top to bottom by the temperature it must be cooked to: ready-to-eat food at the top, then fish, then whole cuts of beef and pork, then ground meats, with raw poultry at the bottom.

blocks.name: cu-shelf
blocks.cap: Put the foods on the shelves in a safe order, top to bottom, then check.

blocks.html: The order works because anything that drips only drips onto food that will be cooked hotter. Chicken juice on the floor of the walk-in can't reach the salad above it; salad juice on chicken does no harm, because the chicken will be cooked to 165°F.

blocks.title: Which shelf?
blocks.q: Where do you store raw ground beef relative to raw salmon?
steps: Ground beef must reach 155°F (Food Code) or 160°F (USDA); fish 145°F.
The higher temperature goes lower.

blocks.html: Using the same tongs for raw chicken going onto the grill and cooked chicken coming off. Use clean tongs, or wash them between.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Rearrange your own refrigerator in the safe order. Put raw meat in a container or on a tray so it can't drip.

blocks.html: For a person with a food allergy, a tiny amount of the wrong food can cause a serious reaction. Cooking does not destroy allergens, so the only protection is keeping them out of the food.

The nine major food allergens named by U.S. law (FDA): milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added by the FASTER Act, signed in 2021, and became a major allergen on January 1, 2023.

items: Know every ingredient in every dish, including sauces, oils, garnishes and store-bought parts.
When a guest says they have an allergy, tell the chef, and use clean tools, boards and pans.
Fryer oil carries allergens: food fried in oil used for shrimp is not safe for a shellfish allergy.
Picking an allergen off a finished plate does not make it safe; remake the dish.
If you don't know, say you don't know and find out. Never guess.

blocks.html: Allergens are a chemical hazard in the Food Code's sense, and they are the one hazard heat can't fix. That is why menus and servers must be able to answer questions honestly.

blocks.title: Safe or not?
blocks.q: A guest is allergic to sesame. The burger bun has sesame seeds; the cook removes the bun and puts the patty on a plain bun.
steps: Seeds and crumbs may already be on the patty.
The safe fix is a new patty and bun prepared with clean tools.
blocks.a: Not safe; start again with clean tools.

blocks.html: Thinking "a little won't hurt". For some people, a trace is enough.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Read the labels in your pantry and find the "Contains" statement on five packages. Which of the nine allergens do you see most?

blocks.html: People are the most common way germs get into food. Good hygiene is the cheapest food safety there is.

Wash hands for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm water, scrubbing backs, between fingers and under nails, then dry with a single-use towel or air dryer. Wash before starting work, after the restroom, after handling raw meat, poultry or seafood, after touching your face, hair, phone, money or trash, after cleaning, and before putting on gloves. Gloves are for ready-to-eat food; change them when they tear, when you switch tasks, and after raw meat.

items: Keep fingernails short and clean; cover cuts with a bandage and a glove.
Hair restrained (hat or net); clean clothes and apron.
No eating, drinking or smoking where food is prepared; a covered drink with a straw may be allowed away from food.
Under the Food Code, workers with vomiting or diarrhea stay away from food work; illnesses such as norovirus spread easily through food.

blocks.html: Bare hands should not touch ready-to-eat food in a restaurant under the Food Code: use gloves, tongs or deli paper. Gloves stop germs only until they touch something dirty.

blocks.title: Change gloves?
blocks.q: You wore gloves to portion raw chicken. Now you need to plate a salad.
steps: Raw chicken contaminated the gloves.
Remove them, wash hands, then put on new gloves.
blocks.a: Yes: take them off, wash your hands, new gloves.

blocks.html: Thinking gloves replace handwashing. Dirty hands make dirty gloves.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Time your handwashing with a clock: 20 seconds is longer than it feels. Hum a short tune twice.
  • Put a little cinnamon or flour on your hands, wash quickly, and look for what you missed.

blocks.html: A surface can look clean and still carry germs. That's why kitchens do two steps.

Cleaning removes food, grease and dirt with soap or detergent and water. Sanitizing reduces germs to a safe level, with heat or a chemical sanitizer, on a surface that is already clean. Mix sanitizer exactly as its label says, check its strength with the test strips made for it, and let it stay wet on the surface for the contact time on the label.

head: Three-compartment sink
What happens
rows: Hot water and detergent; scrub off food
Clean water removes detergent (soap can weaken some sanitizers)
Sanitizer at the label's strength and contact time, or hot water by the code's temperature
blocks.cap: Washing dishes by hand in a commercial kitchen (scrape first)

blocks.html: Food and grease shield germs from sanitizer, and some sanitizers are used up by food soil. Spraying sanitizer on a dirty board does little. Clean first, then sanitize.

blocks.title: Order of steps
blocks.q: A cutting board was used for raw chicken. What do you do before cutting lettuce on it?
steps: Scrape and wash with detergent.
Rinse.
Sanitize as the label says and let it air-dry (or use a different, clean board).

blocks.html:
🛡️ Safety

  • Never mix cleaning chemicals; for example, bleach with ammonia or acids gives off harmful gases.
  • Store chemicals below and away from food, in labeled containers.
  • Read each chemical's safety data sheet and label; wear the gloves or eye protection they call for.
Drying sanitized dishes with a towel. Let them air-dry.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Set up three basins at home (wash, rinse, sanitize) for one evening's dishes, using a sanitizer made for food-contact surfaces and following its label.

blocks.html: HACCP (say "hassip") is a way to plan food safety before anything goes wrong. It started with food for the U.S. space program in the 1960s and is now used by food plants and by restaurants for special processes.

The seven principles: (1) analyze hazards; (2) find the critical control points (CCPs), steps where control is essential, such as cooking and cooling; (3) set critical limits for each (for example, 165°F for poultry); (4) monitor them (who checks, how, how often); (5) set corrective actions when a limit is missed; (6) verify the plan works; (7) keep records.

head: Step for chicken soup
CCP?
Critical limit
rows: 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours; to 41°F within 6 hours in all

blocks.html: The Food Code requires a HACCP plan for some special processes in restaurants, such as reduced-oxygen packaging (vacuum-sealing and sous vide), curing, and smoking to preserve. Most daily cooking is covered by the code's ordinary rules instead.

blocks.title: Corrective action
blocks.q: The cooling log shows soup at 80°F two hours after it was 135°F.
steps: Stage 1's limit (70°F within 2 hours) was missed.
By the Food Code: reheat to 165°F and start cooling again, or discard; then find out why.
blocks.a: Reheat to 165°F and cool again (or discard), and fix the cause.

blocks.html: Calling every step a critical control point. A CCP is where control is essential and the hazard can't be fixed later.

🏠 Practice at home

  • Write a HACCP table for a dish you make, like chili or chicken salad: each step, whether it is a CCP, and its limit.
